articleSummary: Urticaria in children is not synonymous with allergy; viral infections are a common trigger for acute hives. Classic urticaria presents pink or red wheals that itch, appear quickly, and may spread, with each lesion usually resolving within 24 hours without scarring. If hives accompany lip or tongue swelling, vomiting, abdominal pain, wheezing, or breathing difficulty, systemic anaphylaxis must be considered and treated promptly. Recurrent hives with no clear food or medicine trigger, especially during fever, cough, runny nose, or diarrhea, should not be labeled as food allergy. Infections, particularly viruses, can cause hives; bacteria such as group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae may accompany rashes but do not justify antibiotics without confirmed infection. Distinguish fixed lesions lasting more than a day, painful or purplish with bleeding or bullae, from urticaria. Four warning signs: rapid onset with trigger, multisystem symptoms, fixed duration, and fever with purpura requiring urgent evaluation.

articleHeadline: Opinion | How the melting glaciers are unlocking ancient superbugs we've never seen before
articleSummary: Glacial melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) and adjacent regions is releasing ancient pathogens into modern watersheds. Notable events include the 2016 anthrax outbreak on Russia’s Yamal Peninsula—over 2,300 reindeer killed, dozens of people infected, one fatally—linked to thawed permafrost; recent Nepal floods (Bhotekoshi, Aug 26) and a July 2025 transboundary glacial flood triggered in China’s Gyirong County, which destroyed infrastructure and claimed several lives. Scientific work from the Tibetan Plateau (Guliya ice cap) recovered viral genomes up to 15,000 years old, later extended to 41,000 years with about 1,700 viral species, indicating ancient viral diversity; pathogens including Cryptococcus, Aureobasidium melanogenum, Naganishia albida, and Rhodotorula mucilosa were found in Greenland/Svalbard glaciers. A 30,000-year-old Siberian permafrost yielded a vancomycin-resistance gene, showing long-standing antibiotic resistance potential. The piece calls for proactive metagenomic surveillance, eDNA metabarcoding, and One Health-oriented expansion of sequencing to monitor glacier-fed systems and mitigate risks.

articleSummary: Rabies virus is transmitted through the saliva of infected mammals, notably dogs, cats, and bats, affecting both domestic and wild animals. The incubation period generally lasts 2–3 months, but can be as short as 1 week or as long as 1 year, depending on bite location and viral load. Early symptoms mimic general illness (fever, headache, fatigue), with local neuropathic signs around the wound (pain, itching, burning, tingling, numbness), even if the wound has healed. As of 2026-09-11, rabies remains untreatable once symptoms develop.

articleSummary: Skin tuberculosis (cutaneous TB/extrapulmonary TB) is highlighted by a KGMU study in Lucknow, India, analyzing 54 patients aged 20–40 from 2019–2022. About one month after starting therapy, improvements were seen; those completing the full course achieved complete healing of skin lesions. Among the seven drug-resistant cases, four clinical forms emerged: lupus vulgaris (3), scrofuloderma (2), tubercular abscess (1), and tubercular chancre (1). Low bacillary load in skin TB can hinder culture-based detection, underscoring the need for molecular testing (CBNAAT/GeneXpert), culture, and drug-susceptibility testing; whole-genome sequencing may enhance future detection. Early testing and adherence to extended regimens (9–18 months) are crucial to prevent dissemination to chest or brain and relapse with incomplete treatment.
